before.content_html:
Conservation of Energy

The conservation of energy is one of the most important ideas in physics. It states that energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred from one store to another. The total energy in a closed system always stays the same.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. In a closed system, the total energy before a change is always equal to the total energy after the change.

Calculating Gravitational Potential Energy

When an object is raised above the ground, energy is transferred to its gravitational potential energy store. The amount of energy stored depends on the mass, the gravitational field strength, and the height gained:

\(\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h\)

Where \(\Delta GPE\) is the change in gravitational potential energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), \(g\) is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N/kg), and \(\Delta h\) is the change in vertical height in metres (m). On Earth, \(g \approx 9.8\) N/kg.

A 2 kg book is lifted 1.5 m onto a shelf. Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy. Use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg.

\(\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h = 2 \times 9.8 \times 1.5 = 29.4\) J

Calculating Kinetic Energy

The energy in the kinetic energy store of a moving object depends on its mass and the square of its speed:

\(KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2\)

Where \(KE\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in metres per second (m/s). Because speed is squared, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

A 0.5 kg ball travels at 4 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

\(KE = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 4^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 16 = 4\) J

Wasted Energy and Efficiency

No energy transfer is perfectly efficient. Some energy is always dissipated — spread out to the thermal store of the surroundings. This wasted energy cannot easily be recovered. Mechanical processes become wasteful when friction causes a rise in temperature, heating the surroundings.

We can reduce unwanted energy transfers by lubrication (reducing friction between moving parts) and thermal insulation (reducing energy transfer by heating). For example, loft insulation and cavity wall insulation reduce the rate at which a building cools by trapping air, which is a poor thermal conductor.

Key Fact

Efficiency measures how much of the input energy is usefully transferred: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}}\). Efficiency has no units and is always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%).

Energy Resources

The main energy resources available on Earth are: non-renewable sources (fossil fuels — coal, oil, natural gas — and nuclear fuel) and renewable sources (wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave, and bio-fuel).

Non-renewable resources release large amounts of energy per kilogram and provide a reliable supply. However, burning fossil fuels produces carbon dioxide (contributing to climate change) and they will eventually run out. Nuclear fuel produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely.

Renewable resources will not run out and most produce no greenhouse gases during operation. However, many are intermittent (wind and solar depend on weather conditions), and some require large land areas or have visual/noise impacts. Bio-fuels are carbon neutral in theory because the plants absorb CO\(_2\) as they grow.

The global trend is a shift towards renewable energy sources. This is driven by concerns about climate change, energy security (reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels), and the falling cost of renewable technologies such as solar panels and wind turbines.

Key Fact

Non-renewable resources (fossil fuels and nuclear) provide reliable, high-energy output but produce waste and will run out. Renewable resources (wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal, bio-fuel, wave) are replenished naturally but many are intermittent.

Exam Tip: Calculation questions on energy are very common. Always write the equation, substitute the values with correct units, then calculate. Show every step — you can pick up method marks even if you make an arithmetic error. Remember that \(v\) in the kinetic energy equation is squared, so always square the speed before multiplying.

The conservation of energy principle underpins all energy calculations. You need to recall and use the equations for gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, understand efficiency, and be able to compare renewable and non-renewable energy resources.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways unwanted energy transfers can be reduced in mechanical systems.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Lubrication to reduce friction between moving parts (1)
• Thermal insulation to reduce energy loss by heating (1).

practice_questions.text: A student lifts a 3 kg box to a height of 2 m. Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained. Use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Writes or identifies \(\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h\) (1)
• Substitutes correctly: \(3 \times 9.8 \times 2\) (1)
• Gives correct answer: 58.8 J (1).

practice_questions.text: A 0.2 kg tennis ball is hit at a speed of 10 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Writes or identifies \(KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2\) (1)
• Substitutes correctly: \(\frac{1}{2} \times 0.2 \times 10^2\) (1)
• Gives correct answer: 10 J (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the use of fossil fuels and wind energy as energy resources.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Fossil fuels are non-renewable / wind is renewable (1)
• Fossil fuels produce CO\(_2\) / greenhouse gases when burned; wind does not (1)
• Fossil fuels provide a reliable / constant supply; wind is intermittent / depends on weather (1)
• Fossil fuels have high energy density per kg; wind turbines require large areas of land (1).

practice_questions.text: A light bulb is supplied with 100 J of energy each second. It transfers 15 J of energy as light and the rest as heat. Calculate the efficiency of the light bulb and explain why no device can ever be 100% efficient.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 15 ÷ 100 = 0.15 or 15%
• 85 J is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings
• This wasted energy is dissipated and cannot easily be recovered
• All devices transfer some energy to thermal stores through friction, air resistance, or electrical resistance
• Conservation of energy means total energy is conserved, but some is always transferred to less useful stores
• Therefore no real device can be 100% efficient

Mastering (5–6 marks): Correct calculation with clear, detailed explanation using correct terminology.
Secure (3–4 marks): Correct calculation with some explanation of wasted energy.
Developing (1–2 marks): Attempts calculation or provides basic explanation.

glossary_terms.definition: A fundamental principle stating that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.
A system where no energy can enter or leave — the total energy stays the same.
The force of gravity acting on each kilogram of mass — on Earth this is approximately 9.8 N/kg.
The energy stored in a moving object — depends on mass and the square of its speed.
Energy that has been transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and is no longer in a useful form.
The proportion of input energy that is usefully transferred — always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%).
Using a substance such as oil or grease to reduce friction between moving surfaces.
Using materials with low thermal conductivity to reduce the rate of energy transfer by heating.
Energy resources that will eventually run out because they are used faster than they form — includes coal, oil, natural gas, and nuclear fuel.
Energy resources that will not run out because they are replenished naturally — includes wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, and bio-fuel.

before.content_html:
Energy Transferred by Electrical Devices

Every electrical device transfers energy from one store to another. A kettle transfers energy from the electrical store to the thermal store of water. A motor transfers energy from the electrical store to the kinetic store. Understanding how much energy a device transfers — and how quickly — is essential for calculating running costs and choosing appropriate safety features.

The energy transferred by a device depends on three things: the current flowing through it, the potential difference across it, and how long it runs for. These are linked by the equation:

$$E = I \times V \times t$$

where \(E\) is energy transferred in joules (J), \(I\) is current in amperes (A), \(V\) is potential difference in volts (V), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s). For example, a heater drawing 10 A at 230 V for 60 seconds transfers \(10 \times 230 \times 60 = 138{,}000\) J of energy.

Key Fact

Energy transferred (J) = current (A) × potential difference (V) × time (s). You must be able to recall and rearrange this equation.

Electrical Power

Power tells you how fast a device transfers energy. It is measured in watts (W), where one watt equals one joule of energy transferred per second. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J every second — much faster than a 60 W lamp, which transfers only 60 J per second.

Power is calculated using:

$$P = \frac{E}{t}$$

where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) is energy transferred in joules (J), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s).

Two more equations link power to current, potential difference, and resistance:

$$P = I \times V$$

$$P = I^2 \times R$$

The second equation shows that doubling the current quadruples the power dissipated, because current is squared. This is why high-current devices need thicker cables — thin wires carrying large currents would overheat dangerously.

Key Fact

Three power equations to recall: \(P = \frac{E}{t}\), \(P = I \times V\), and \(P = I^2 \times R\). Each connects power to different electrical quantities.

Direct Current and Alternating Current

There are two types of electric current. Direct current (d.c.) is the movement of charge in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply d.c. — the current always flows from the positive terminal, through the circuit, and back to the negative terminal.

Alternating current (a.c.) is different: the direction of charge flow keeps reversing. In the UK, the mains electricity supply is a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz (meaning the current changes direction 50 times per second) and a voltage of about 230 V.

Alternating current can be easily stepped up to very high voltages for efficient long-distance transmission through the National Grid, then stepped back down for safe domestic use. Transformers, which only work with a.c., make this possible. Direct current cannot be transformed in the same way, which is why a.c. became the standard for mains supply.

The Three-Pin Plug and Mains Wiring

Domestic appliances connect to the mains through a three-pin plug containing three colour-coded wires:

The live wire (brown) carries the alternating current to the appliance. Its potential alternates between about +230 V and −230 V relative to the neutral wire. This makes it dangerous even when a device is switched off — the live wire is still connected to the supply.

The neutral wire (blue) completes the circuit and carries current away from the appliance. It is at, or very close to, 0 V (earth potential).

The earth wire (green and yellow stripes) is a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. Under normal conditions, no current flows through it. If a fault occurs and the live wire touches the metal casing, the earth wire provides a low-resistance path for current to flow safely to earth, preventing electrocution.

Key Fact

Live wire = brown (alternates at ~230 V). Neutral wire = blue (~0 V). Earth wire = green and yellow (safety, connected to metal casing). The potential difference between live and neutral is about 230 V. Between live and earth it is also about 230 V. Between neutral and earth it is approximately 0 V.

Fuses and Circuit Breakers

A fuse is a thin wire inside a ceramic or glass case, placed in series with the live wire. If the current exceeds the fuse's rated value, the wire melts and breaks the circuit, cutting off the current before it can cause a fire or damage the appliance. Common fuse ratings are 3 A (for appliances up to about 700 W) and 13 A (for higher-power devices).

Fuses and switches must always be connected in the live wire, not the neutral wire. This ensures that when the fuse blows or the switch is off, no high voltage reaches the appliance — making it safe to touch or repair.

A circuit breaker does the same job but works faster and can be reset by flipping a switch, rather than needing to be replaced like a fuse.

If the fuse were in the neutral wire and it blew, the live wire would still be connected to the appliance. The metal casing could remain at 230 V, creating a serious electrocution risk. By placing the fuse in the live wire, blowing the fuse disconnects the high-voltage supply completely.

Power Ratings and Energy Use

Every domestic appliance has a power rating printed on it. A 2000 W kettle uses energy much faster than a 10 W LED bulb. Higher power means greater energy transfer per second, which usually means higher running costs.

Different appliances transfer energy in different ways. A toaster transfers electrical energy to thermal energy to heat bread. A washing machine transfers electrical energy to kinetic energy (the drum spinning) and thermal energy (heating the water). A television transfers electrical energy to light and sound energy.

To calculate the current drawn by an appliance, rearrange \(P = I \times V\) to give \(I = \frac{P}{V}\). For a 2000 W kettle on the 230 V mains: \(I = \frac{2000}{230} \approx 8.7\) A. This tells you a 13 A fuse is needed (the next standard rating above 8.7 A).

Calculate the normal operating current using \(I = \frac{P}{V}\), then choose the fuse with the next rating above this value. For a 700 W microwave: \(I = \frac{700}{230} \approx 3.0\) A, so a 3 A fuse is suitable. For a 2500 W heater: \(I = \frac{2500}{230} \approx 10.9\) A, so a 13 A fuse is needed. The fuse must be rated just above the normal current — too low and it blows during normal use; too high and it fails to protect.

Dangers of the Mains Supply

The mains supply at 230 V is potentially lethal. Any connection between the live wire and earth creates a direct path for current to flow through whatever — or whoever — completes that circuit. Touching the live wire while standing on the ground can cause a large current to pass through the body, which can cause burns, cardiac arrest, or death.

Even when a switch is off, the live wire inside the appliance may still be at 230 V. This is why you should always switch off and unplug an appliance before attempting any repairs, and why damaged cables or cracked plugs must be replaced immediately.

Key Fact

The live wire is dangerous because it carries a potential of ~230 V even when a switch is off. Any connection between live and earth can cause electrocution. Safety features include: fuses in the live wire, earth wires on metal-cased appliances, circuit breakers, and double insulation on plastic-cased devices.

Exam Tip

When asked to explain why a fuse must be in the live wire, always state that it disconnects the high-voltage supply from the appliance. Simply saying "it breaks the circuit" is not enough — you must explain that the appliance is no longer connected to 230 V.

Summary

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts. The UK mains supply is a.c. at 230 V and 50 Hz. Domestic plugs have three wires (live, neutral, earth) with fuses and circuit breakers providing safety. Understanding power ratings helps you calculate current draw, choose the correct fuse, and compare energy use between appliances.
